They will repel the invasion and destroy the invaders. So, how do we get this culture? The education system of the Spartans is really interesting—actually disturbing. Young boys at age five and six are taken away from their homes and placed in a school run by older boys, around 10 to 11 years old. As you can imagine, the older boys beat up the younger ones viciously. From day one, there's no education; they're not learning anything. All that happens is the older boys are beating the younger ones.

But because this hazing builds solidarity and brotherhood, young boys who are five and six learn to love each other by helping each other survive the brutality. When these boys turn 11 to 13 during puberty, they become mentored by an older Spartan soldier, maybe around 28 to 30 years old with a family. They form intimate relationships, engaging in sex, which further builds group solidarity. During this hazing phase, young boys learn to trust and bond with each other.

By age 18, they graduate. To do so, they have a mission: the Spartans enslave people called Helots, former captives working in the fields under harsh rules, including strict curfews. If caught outside after dark, Helots face execution. As part of their graduation, young soldiers hide in the fields at night, waiting for late Helots to cut their throats as a form of human sacrifice. This practice builds group cohesion and unification.

Other city-states like Thebes copied the Spartan system but made it voluntary. They called it the Sacred Band, consisting of 300 soldiers who were lovers, which was not considered homosexuality in that era. These units became dominant military forces after Sparta, with the Sacred Band of Thieves leading the way as vanguards and spearheads in battles.

Finally, Macedonia adopted this system, led by Alexander the Great, Philip II's son, who built the greatest army in history.
